resources.string: Blockfy uses Accessibility to leave short-video screens and, with adult blocking on, to check the address bar of your browser against a list of adult sites. It does not read messages, chats, or anything you type in other apps, and does not save what it reads.

Blockfy only works with Accessibility turned on. It uses this permission to detect and leave short-video screens (Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, X) and to count time in those apps. If you turn on adult blocking, it also reads your browser\'s address bar to check the site you are visiting against a list of adult sites. It never reads messages, chats, passwords, or anything typed inside other apps, and does not save or send what it reads. Blockfy does not open banking apps. By tapping Accept you agree to this use.

1. Open app info and allow restricted settings, if the phone asks.
2. Open Accessibility settings.
3. Under downloaded apps, tap Blockfy.
4. Turn the service on and confirm.

resources.string: Blocking buys you breathing room. What changes your life is what you come to believe about yourself and what you do next. Read in order. No rush, and no lying to yourself.
You are not weak. You are up against a product built to keep you.
What it takes from your character, your relationships and your freedom.

string-array.name: concept_shorts_titles
string-array.item: You are not weak. You are up against a product
One more, and one more, and one more
You train what you repeat
Your work gets shallow
Sleep and mood pay the bill
Other people\'s showcase versus your whole day
You can get out, and it is lighter than it looks

string-array.name: concept_shorts_bodies
string-array.item: Whole teams of engineers and data scientists work so that you stay one more minute. Every swipe is measured, tested and tuned. If you feel you cannot stop, that does not prove you are weak: it proves the product works. But knowing that does not take your responsibility away. Now that you know, the question is: what are you going to do about it?

There is no last episode. The next video is already loaded, picked because it is the one most likely to hold you. No video ends in a way that makes you stand up. The product is not the video. The product is your attention, sold in batches. Until you decide the limit, someone else decides it for you.

With every short video you train yourself to expect something new every few seconds. The more you train, the duller reading, talking, working or sitting in silence feels. The world did not get boring: your reward system got spoiled. The good news is that what is learned can be unlearned, and many people feel a difference after a few weeks away from the feed.

Every time you drop a task to peek at the feed, your focus takes a while to come back. People who keep interrupting themselves deliver half-done work and end the day more tired. The thing you say you have no time for is often buried under a pile of videos.

Scrolling at night steals the sleep that would make tomorrow easier. You wake up more irritable, with less patience, and more likely to open the same app again. It is a loop: tiredness asks for the feed, and the feed adds to the tiredness.

You see the best minute of thousands of people\'s lives, edited, filtered and rehearsed, and compare it with your whole unedited day. You always lose. That feeling of falling behind is not information about your life. It is a side effect of staring at other people\'s showcase.

The first week is the worst: your hand goes to the phone on its own and your body asks for the stimulus. After that the urge usually fades. Many people report more calm, more sleep and more drive in the first weeks. You are not giving up something valuable. You are trading what consumes you for what builds you.

string-array.name: concept_porn_titles
string-array.item: It trains you to use people
Character wears down in secret
You do not know who you are watching
The shame cycle
Relationships cool off
Sex life shrinks
You can get out, and you will recognize yourself

string-array.name: concept_porn_bodies
string-array.item: Pornography teaches you to treat another person as a product: available, silent and discarded when the feeling passes. That habit does not stay on the screen. It shows in how you look at people who are really there with you. Every click is practice, and you are always practicing something.

Doing this in secret splits you in two. You say one thing about who you are and keep another life you would not defend out loud. Character is what you repeat when no one is judging you. The secret weighs more than the act, and the longer it lasts, the more it costs.

Part of this content involves exploitation, coercion or people who never agreed to be seen. You have no way of knowing which. Every click feeds an industry where someone\'s suffering can be the product. It is hard to keep saying "I do not hurt anyone" while looking at that squarely.

The cycle is usually: tension, use, short relief, shame, tension again. Shame does not pull you away from the habit: it creates the stress that asks for the next relief. That is why punishing yourself does not work. What breaks the cycle is the next action: leave the room, call someone, go back to the plan.

A partnership is not a stream of novelty. If your arousal starts to depend on strangers, tabs and going further and further, the person who loves you starts to look insufficient. That is not their failing. It is the price of the habit. And the person beside you often feels more than you imagine.

Heavy use can make real intimacy slower, more anxious or harder to enjoy. Many people report needing more intensity for the same effect, until an ordinary body beside them stops being enough. That is not a high standard: it is a dysregulated appetite, and appetite can be retrained.

If you are set on it, you will find a way around any block. The block exists to create a pause: enough time to remember this does not give you a better life, a clearer head or a relationship you respect. The first weeks are the hardest. After that, many people describe more clarity and more presence. Relapses happen; what counts is the direction.

What Blockfy is, and what it is not.

Blockfy was made to help people who want to cut down habits that became hard to control: endless short videos, pornography and too much phone use. It can also help people who deal with compulsions, screen dependence and trouble focusing, as in ADHD. It works by putting barriers and limits on your phone.

No app changes a habit by itself. Blockfy blocks, warns and limits, but you are the one who decides to keep going. There will be hard days, and you will be able to turn blocks off. The result depends on your will, on a routine and on the people around you.
If it does not get better, get help

Blockfy is not a treatment, does not diagnose anything and does not replace professional care. If a bad habit persists, gets in the way of your life or causes you suffering, it is worth seeing a psychologist or a psychiatrist. In Brazil, CVV answers on 188, free, 24 hours a day. Elsewhere, search for your country\'s emotional support line.
How a habit becomes a compulsion, and what to do when the urge hits.
Tips for trouble paying attention, with or without a diagnosis.
Simple steps to set Blockfy up and keep going.
Signs that an app alone is not enough, and where to find support.

string-array.name: concept_habits_titles
string-array.item: The urge passes

string-array.name: concept_habits_bodies
string-array.item: An urge usually rises, peaks and fades within minutes, even if you do nothing. Waiting 10 to 20 minutes while doing something else takes much of its strength away. When the urge comes, tell yourself: "I will wait 15 minutes." Often it has already passed.

Every habit has a trigger (boredom, anxiety, tiredness, the phone in your hand), a routine (opening the app) and a reward (quick relief). To change it, find your trigger and swap the routine instead of only fighting the urge. Write it down for a few days: when and why do you open the app?

The more steps between you and the impulse, the less you give in. Keep the phone away from your bed, take the apps off your home screen and keep Blockfy on. That is what a block is for: turning a two-tap impulse into something hard to do.

The feed was built to have no end. Deciding the limit before you open the app, and letting the app enforce it, works better than deciding in the moment, when the urge is already strong. People who decide in the heat of the moment tend to lose.

Forbidding without offering something else leaves a gap. Have an alternative ready for your riskiest hours: a walk, calling someone, a book, a shower, a board game, exercise. Plan it before you need it.

Relapsing does not erase what you already gained. What hurts is giving up everything after a slip. Noticed you slipped? Get back to the plan the same day, without punishing yourself. Too much guilt tends to feed the cycle instead of breaking it.
Secrets feed compulsion. Having one trusted person who knows your goal usually helps you keep the commitment on bad days. It can be a friend, a relative or a professional.

string-array.name: concept_focus_titles
string-array.item: Blockfy does not diagnose
Short videos train distraction
Fewer decisions, more ready-made rules
One step at a time
Sleep, food and movement
Treatment is for professionals

string-array.name: concept_focus_bodies
string-array.item: Trouble paying attention can have many causes: ADHD, anxiety, depression, poor sleep, too much screen time, stress. Only a health professional can assess your case. Blockfy helps with your environment (less distraction), not with a diagnosis.

Switching stimulus every few seconds can get the brain used to quick rewards, and long tasks start to feel harder and duller. Cutting the endless feed is often one of the most effective steps to get your concentration back.

People who struggle with attention often benefit from ready-made rules: fixed hours, automatic limits, few choices in the moment. Setting Blockfy up once saves willpower later, because you do not have to decide every time.

Split the task into blocks of 10 to 25 minutes with a short break between them. Keep the phone in another room during the block. Start with the smallest possible piece: the hard part is usually starting, not continuing.
Sleeping badly worsens attention and impulse control. Physical activity, daylight and regular meals help. Before blaming a lack of discipline, look at the basics of your body.

If you have or suspect ADHD, treatment is decided with a psychiatrist, neurologist or psychologist, and may include therapy and, when indicated, medication. No app replaces that. Never start or stop a medication on your own.

string-array.name: concept_plan_titles
string-array.item: Write your reason

A limit you can keep
App limit vs Reels limit
Hours that protect you

string-array.name: concept_plan_bodies
string-array.item: Before you set anything up, write in one sentence why you want to change. In the Concepts tab, tap "My reason". It shows on your home screen and at the moment you try to give up. When the urge speaks loud, it is your own calm, honest voice that will answer.
Turn on just one or two apps at first. A limit you keep is worth more than ten you switch off. When it gets easy, add the next one.

If you use 3 hours a day today, start with 2 and lower it week by week. An impossible limit only leads to turning the block off and giving up. Protect your clean-day streak: it is worth more than any extra minute.

You can have, for example, 1 hour of Instagram a day but only 15 minutes of Reels. It is the most realistic combination: you keep what is useful (messages, friends, work) and cut the endless feed. Set it in each app: one rule for the whole app and another for Reels/Shorts.
Nights are often the riskiest hours. In Settings, choose the days and hours when blocks apply, for example the Night preset. The hours are the same for every app.
Turn on strict mode in a moment of motivation. Until midnight you can only make blocks stricter, never looser. It is an agreement you make with yourself before the urge arrives.
Once a week, look at your streak, your blocks and what worked. Adjust what is too hard or too easy. The goal is not a perfect app setup: it is to have time and attention left for what matters to you.

string-array.name: concept_help_bodies
string-array.item: Blockfy builds barriers. It does not treat the cause of the habit, which can be anxiety, loneliness, depression, trauma, ADHD or something else. If the cause is still there, the urge tends to come back another way.

It is worth seeing a professional if: you try to stop and cannot, several times; the habit gets in the way of work, studies, sleep or relationships; you feel intense guilt, shame or anxiety; you use the habit to escape bad emotions; you hide it or lie about it; or your mood is very low.

A psychologist does therapy (for example cognitive-behavioral), which helps you understand triggers and build strategies. A psychiatrist is a medical doctor: assesses and diagnoses conditions such as ADHD, depression and anxiety, and can prescribe medication when needed. Many people use both. If you are unsure where to start, start with either one.

Look for your local public health clinic or a mental health service. In Brazil, CVV (188, free, 24 hours) offers emotional support by phone, chat and email, and the public system (SUS) has UBS clinics and CAPS centers. Elsewhere, search for your country\'s emotional support line.

Get help now: call your local emergency number or crisis line, or go to the nearest emergency room. In Brazil, call CVV on 188 or SAMU on 192. You do not have to go through this alone, and this feeling can improve with support.

Asking for help is not weakness or exaggeration. The sooner you look for it, the simpler the path usually is. This app can stay by your side, but people and professionals are what make the difference.

string-array.name: concept_time_titles
string-array.item: Do the math

The cost that does not show
The most common regret

string-array.name: concept_time_bodies
string-array.item: Two hours a day on the phone is 14 hours a week and about 730 hours a year: more than 30 full 24-hour days, every year. Three hours a day is over 45 days a year. Look at your average and multiply by 365. That is the part of your life you hand over every year.

Keeping your current average for ten years, that is 300 to 450 whole days of your life looking at a screen, close to a year or more without sleeping. What book, course, body, business or relationship would fit in that time? This is not exaggeration for effect. It is just arithmetic.

If someone gave you 700 free hours a year, what would you do? Learning a language well takes, for many people, hundreds of hours. Changing your body, starting a business, finishing a course: it all fits in hours. You already have those hours. They are just going somewhere else.

Time in the feed does not show up as a cost anywhere. No one bills you, you do not feel you lost anything. It is the most expensive cost there is precisely because it is invisible. You can earn money back. You cannot earn years back.

Hardly anyone near the end of life says they regret looking at their phone less. Regret is usually about what was not done: the person not visited, the project left in a drawer, the time not lived. Today you can still choose differently.

You do not need to win everything back today. Win back one hour. One hour a day is 365 hours a year, over 15 days. Pick one thing that matters to you, put that hour on your calendar and protect it like a non-negotiable commitment. That is how a life changes: one hour at a time.

string-array.name: concept_mindset_titles
string-array.item: What you believe already decides for you
You are not your habit
The brain is not destiny
Every block kept is a vote
Discomfort is the training
Stop bargaining in the moment
Responsibility without guilt

string-array.name: concept_mindset_bodies
string-array.item: If you believe you are an addict and will be like this forever, every slip becomes proof and every hard day becomes a sentence. If you believe you are learning to change, the same slip becomes information. Same situation, two stories, two futures. You do not choose the facts of your past, but you choose the story you tell about them. Start by swapping "I am like this" for "I am learning to be different".

"I am an addict" is an identity. "I have a habit I am changing" is a situation. Identity sticks; situations change. For some people, acknowledging the problem in support groups is an important part of the path, and that is valid. The point here is different: do not turn the problem into a sentence. You are much bigger than the worst thing you do.

The brain keeps adapting throughout life. What you repeat gets stronger; what you stop repeating gets weaker. That is true for the bad habit and for the new one. It is not magic and it is not fast, but it is real: every time you choose differently, you strengthen the new path and weaken the old one.

Every time you keep what you agreed with yourself, you vote for who you want to be: someone who keeps their word. You do not have to win the election today. You only need more votes than your old self. In 30 days you will have concrete evidence that you are that person. Self-trust is not declared: it is built, one clean day at a time.

The restlessness that squeezes is the discomfort of a habit being undone, not a sign that you are wrong. People who wait to feel good before changing never change. You will miss it, you will be bored, you will not know what to do with your hands. Getting through that is the training, the same discomfort as building muscle. When it hurts, remember: this is how it works.

You will not feel like changing when the urge of the habit arrives. So decide beforehand, without depending on willpower. Simple rules set with a calm head reduce the battle in the moment. "If I feel like opening the feed, then I stand up and drink a glass of water." Research on implementation intentions suggests this kind of if-then helps people do what they planned.

Being hard on yourself is not humiliating yourself. It is owning it: "this is on me, and I can change." Guilt looks back and paralyzes. Responsibility looks forward and acts. You are not to blame for what the product was designed to do. But you are responsible for what you do from now on. And that is the best news: what depends on you is exactly what can change.

string-array.name: concept_relapse_titles
string-array.item: You will slip. Plan for it
The "since I already ruined it" effect
Shame feeds it; clarity solves it
Starting over is not going back to zero
Thought about turning the block off? That is a signal
When relapses become a pattern

string-array.name: concept_relapse_bodies
string-array.item: Almost everyone who changes a hard habit slips along the way. It is not an exception: it is part of the process. Decide now what you will do the day after a slip. People with a plan to come back return faster, and people without one are often gone for weeks.

"Since I already broke the streak, I might as well." That thought turns a ten-minute slip into a lost week. The slip happens. What decides the outcome is the second click, the second hour. Stop at the first. Closing the screen right after is a win, even on the worst day.

Shame asks for relief, and the easiest relief is the same habit. Instead of punishing yourself, ask: what happened before? Tiredness, boredom, a fight, loneliness, late night? Write the trigger down. Every well-analysed relapse is a map of what you need to protect.

The streak goes back to zero. What you learned does not. Every clean day taught you something about your triggers, your hours and your defenses. Starting over is starting with more information than last time. And today is the first day of a new streak, which could be the biggest one yet.

If you thought about turning Blockfy off, something is pressing on you: anxiety, boredom, tiredness, an argument. The problem is not the block, it is what is asking for it to get out of the way. Wait 15 minutes. Drink water. Talk to someone. Then decide. If you still turn it off, turn it back on the same day.

If you try and cannot, many times, even though you really want to, that is not a character flaw. It may be a sign that something lies underneath, such as anxiety, depression, ADHD or trauma, and help from a psychologist or psychiatrist shortens the path a lot. Asking for help is not giving up: it is the most efficient decision there is.
